report:
# Conclusion

The claim that taking ibuprofen for COVID-19 worsens the infection is **not supported by evidence** and is considered largely debunked.

Early in the pandemic (March 2020), French Health Minister Olivier Véran raised concern that NSAIDs like ibuprofen might worsen COVID-19, based on a theoretical hypothesis published in *The Lancet* suggesting anti-inflammatories could increase ACE2 receptor expression, potentially facilitating viral entry ([sciencealert.com](https://www.sciencealert.com/who-recommends-to-avoid-taking-ibuprofen-for-covid-19-symptoms)). This triggered global concern and temporary shifts in guidance.

However, the World Health Organization subsequently clarified that it does **not recommend avoiding ibuprofen**, stating there is no evidence linking its use to worsened COVID-19 outcomes ([cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/ibuprofen-covid-19-novel-coronavirus-1.5501496)).

Subsequent large-scale clinical research supports this reassessment. A 38-center observational study of COVID-19 inpatients found NSAID use was **not associated with increased severity**, mortality, invasive ventilation, acute kidney injury, or ECMO use ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9107579/)). Some analyses even found NSAID use correlated with *decreased* mortality and severity, though causal claims remain cautious due to observational study limitations. A systematic review in *The Lancet Rheumatology* similarly found "most previous observational studies have supported the lack of association between NSAID use and COVID-19 severity" ([thelancet.com](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanrhe/article/PIIS2665-9913(21)00144-2/fulltext)).

**Bottom line:** The ibuprofen-worsens-COVID-19 claim originated from a theoretical hypothesis, not confirmed data. Subsequent clinical evidence and major health authorities (including WHO) have found no credible link between ibuprofen use and worsened COVID-19 outcomes.
